paragraphs.source_en: The smile on Lord Ieyasu’s face at once lit Munenori’s heart. Until then, something had always seemed to weigh upon Ieyasu’s heart, leaving his expression gloomy. But from the moment he left Kawagoe Castle, he suddenly became cheerful. The change in Ieyasu was astonishing: yesterday his face had been clouded, yet today it shone like sunlight. Could it be merely because Tenkai had agreed to invite an imperial prince to journey east?

paragraphs.source_en: Ieyasu’s physical weariness had not abated; it was worsening by the day. Yet now not a trace of melancholy could be seen in his eyes; they shone as brightly as a child’s. Only later did Munenori learn that Ieyasu’s relief came not merely from entrusting the matter to Tenkai. More importantly, he had by then achieved the purpose of his hunt. paragraphs.source_en: Ieyasu returned to Edo Castle on the twenty-seventh and then spent six days with Takechiyo in the Western Gardens. This was the last time Iemitsu, the future third shogun, would see his grandfather, and he gazed at Ieyasu in rapt fascination. In the sensitive boy’s eyes, his grandfather was then a mighty tree radiating immeasurable splendor beneath the sun. Perhaps for that very reason, he would later commission more than ten portraits of Lord Ieyasu and build the supremely magnificent Nikkō Tōshō-gū. But that belongs to a later part of the story.
